sources.claim: A diff compares two explicitly named states, such as working tree to index, index to HEAD, or one commit to another, and reports line-oriented changes rather than intent.

canonicalExplanation.summary: A diff always compares **two named states**. `git diff` compares working tree with index (unstaged edits). `git diff --staged` compares index with HEAD (what the next commit will contain). `git diff main..feature` or `git diff A B` compares two commits. Lines starting with `-` were removed and `+` were added, inside **hunks** marked `@@`. A diff shows **what** lines changed, not **why**, and untracked files never appear. Use `--stat` for the file list, `-w` to hide whitespace-only churn, and read every hunk looking for unintended files, noise and real behaviour changes.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner edits two files, stages one, then runs `git diff` to check what they're about to commit. It shows only the unstaged file, and they commit believing the other change isn't included. git diff reviews unstaged edits while git diff --staged reviews the snapshot proposed for the next commit. In this lesson you'll review a patch for unintended files, whitespace-only churn and behavior changes.

```predict
{"question": "You create a brand-new file, don't add it, and run git diff. Does it appear?", "options": ["Yes, as all + lines", "No: untracked files aren't in either compared state"], "answer": 1, "why": "Use git status to see untracked files, or add them and use git diff --staged."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Selective staging and first commit**, **Working tree, index and HEAD**, and **Log, show and graph**.

sections.heading: The distinction: which two states?
sections.body:
```bash
git diff                      # working tree vs index (unstaged).
git diff --staged             # index vs HEAD (next commit).
git diff HEAD                 # working tree vs HEAD (both).
git diff main..feature        # tip of main vs tip of feature.
git diff --stat --staged      # files and line counts only.
git diff -w                   # ignore whitespace-only changes.
```

```diff
@@ -12,3 +12,4 @@ function total(items) {
-  return items.reduce((a, b) => a + b.price);
+  return items.reduce((a, b) => a + b.price, 0);
+  console.log("debug");     // unintended: remove before committing.
```

| Look for | Why |
|---|---|
| files you didn't mean to touch. | accidental edits, lockfile churn. |
| whitespace-only hunks. | noise that hides real changes. |
| changed conditions and returns. | real behaviour changes. |
| debug lines and secrets. | should never be committed. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "What does `@@ -12,3 +12,4 @@` mean?", "answer": "The hunk starts at line 12 and covers 3 lines in the old version and 4 in the new: one line was added overall."}
```

sections.heading: Review the right diff

includes: Choose the right diff for unstaged, staged or commit-to-commit comparisons.
Read hunks for unintended files, whitespace churn, debug lines and behaviour changes.

outcomes: Review a patch for unintended files, whitespace-only churn and behavior changes.

examples.title: Reviewing before the commit
examples.situation: git diff reviews unstaged edits while git diff --staged reviews the snapshot proposed for the next commit.
walkthrough: **Unstaged edits:** git diff shows only styles.css, which isn't staged.
**Snapshot proposed for the next commit:** git diff --staged reveals cart.js plus a stray console.log.
**Fix:** remove the debug line, re-add, and git diff --staged will show only the intended fix.
examples.result: The learner reviews the right comparison and commits only intended lines.

examples.title: The 800-line formatting patch
examples.situation: A pull request diff shows 800 changed lines, but the author says they fixed one condition.
walkthrough: git diff -w main..feature hides the whitespace-only reformatting.
What's left is the single real change: `<` became `<=`.
Ask for the formatting to go in its own commit so the fix is reviewable.
examples.result: The real behaviour change is found and reviewed instead of lost in noise.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: One diff command always shows every change in the repository, including staged, unstaged, and untracked content.
misconceptions.correction: Each diff compares exactly two states. Plain git diff misses staged changes, --staged misses unstaged ones, and neither shows untracked files.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why didn't the new file appear?

analogy.example: A diff is like **comparing two photos of the same room**. You must say which two photos: this morning vs now, or yesterday vs this morning. And an object that's never been photographed (untracked) can't show up in either.
limitations: Photos show what moved, not why; so do diffs.
Rearranged furniture (whitespace) can hide the one thing that actually changed.

steps.explanation: git diff reviews unstaged edits only.
git diff --staged reviews the snapshot proposed for the next commit.
After removing the debug line, the staged diff matches the intent.

nearTransfer.prompt: In a disposable repo, make one staged change, one unstaged change and one untracked file. Predict what git diff, git diff --staged and git diff HEAD show, then check.

farTransfer.prompt: Review a supplied branch against main. Produce a short review listing unintended files, whitespace-only hunks (using -w to confirm) and every behaviour change, with the diff command you used for each finding.
scaffold: Then read hunks with and without -w.

remediation.explanation: Before reading any diff, name the **two states** it compares. Then scan with --stat, filter noise with -w, and read every remaining hunk for behaviour.

recap.summary: To review a patch, pick the diff that compares the two states you care about (git diff for unstaged, --staged for the next commit, A..B for commits), check --stat for unintended files, use -w to strip whitespace churn, and read each hunk for real behaviour changes, remembering untracked files never appear.
